title: רב מארי בר רחל בת שמואל

paragraphs:
Rav Mari bar Raḥel, son of Raḥel, daughter of Shemuel bar Abba the priest. Bava Metzia 103a has 'Rav Meri, son of Shemuel's daughter'; also Shabbat 88b, and the matter in Gittin 36b, 'Rav'—should read Mari—'son of Shemuel's daughter.' Shemuel's daughter was captured and became pregnant by a gentile, who afterward converted and was named Issur the convert (see his entry). Rav Meri's conception was outside Israel's sanctity, but his birth within it. Out of respect for him they designated him by his mother: so Rashi writes in Eizehu Neshekh 73b. Tosafot says he lived in Rava's time, as appears here: Rav Meri bar Raḥel received that house as security, and its owner then sold it to Rava, etc. Bava Batra 149a: Issur the convert had thirteen thousand zuz with Rava (see his entry). In HaḤoletz 45b one should not read 'Rav declared Rav Meri bar Raḥel fit,' but 'Rava declared him fit'; he was Issur the convert's son. (Shabbat 124b: he came before Rava. Berakhot 16a: Rav Meri, son of Shemuel's daughter, raised a contradiction before Rava, who was silent. He asked, 'Have you heard anything on this?' He answered, 'Thus Rav Sheshet said.' Rashi explains that several places call him bar Raḥel; she was Shemuel's daughter and was captured, etc. Sukkah 46a: 'I saw Rava.' Ḥullin 112b: he came before Rava.) We also find another Rav Meri bar Raḥel, Rabbah's son: Shabbat 154a says 'Rabbah, father of Rav Meri bar Raḥel.' End of quotation.

Tosafot, Bava Batra there, writes concerning the statement that Rav Meri bar Raḥel was conceived outside sanctity: HaḤoletz, cited above, says they declared him fit and appointed him to the pursi of Babylonia, etc.; since his mother was an Israelite, 'from among your brothers' applies to him. This person certainly was a convert and could be the one here, Issur the convert's son. But Shabbat 154 describes a full Israelite, saying 'Rabbah, father of Rav Meri bar Raḥel.' Necessarily there were two. Yet Rashbam's statement that Rav Meri was the son of Issur the convert, who had intercourse with Shemuel's captured daughter before converting, so that his conception was outside Israel's sanctity, as related in Ketubbot, seems wrong. R. Yoḥanan—should read Ḥanina—told Rav Shemen bar Abba (see his entry), 'Go attend to your kinswoman, for she is pure.' It therefore seems that the Rav Meri, son of Shemuel's daughter, mentioned elsewhere was someone else, perhaps the Shabbat figure. They name him through his mother to trace him to Shemuel, just as Ravna Ukva and Ravna Neḥemyah were sons of Rav's daughter, and similarly R. Shimon ben Pazi and Abba Shaul ben Imma Miryam. End of quotation; see there.

Shabbat there has 'Rava, brother of Rav Meri bar Raḥel'; some say 'Rava, father of Rav Meri bar Raḥel.' On the latter formulation—Rava his father—the report that Rav declared him fit and appointed him to the pursi of Babylonia, etc., is difficult. Perhaps there were two Meris bar Raḥel. Rashi says not to read 'Some say his father'; whoever does read it also reads 'On the latter formulation,' etc. Tosafot likewise excludes 'Some say his father,' for his father was demonstrably a convert: Rav declared his son Meri fit and appointed him over Babylonia's pursi because his mother was Israelite, etc. One cannot say Rava, Meri's father, was also a convert; he would have been called Rava the convert, like Issur the convert. Moreover, Bava Batra there indicates that Meri bar Raḥel's father was Issur: Issur the convert had, etc., and his son Rav Meri was conceived outside sanctity. Although it does not there read 'Rav Meri bar Raḥel, his son,' it seems he was that person. If so, Issur must have had intercourse with Raḥel daughter of Mar Shemuel before converting. Ketubbot 23 says 'the daughters of Shemuel's daughter' were captured [the source's wording is retained]; perhaps he then had intercourse with her. Although they came before R. Ḥanina and said, 'I was captured and am pure,' not all of them said it.

(This requires examination: Ketubbot 23 says Shemuel's daughters were captured, entered R. Ḥanina's study house, and this one said 'I was captured and am pure,' and the other said the same; he told Rav Shemen bar Abba to attend to his kinswomen. This seems to mean all said it. One cannot explain that a third daughter did not say 'I am pure' and bore Meri bar Raḥel: Tosafot, Bava Batra there, objects to Rashbam's account of Meri's conception outside sanctity precisely because R. Ḥanina told Rav Shemen to attend to his kinswomen. On that proposed explanation, Meri might have been born to the one who did not say she was pure.)

Still, if Issur's son Meri was the one in Yevamot, HaḤoletz, how did Issur live so long, from Rav's time to Rava's? The reading before the writer was 'Rav declared Meri fit,' etc. Rav Yehudah was Rav's student, and Rava was born when Rav Yehudah died. Even Meri himself was already very great in Torah in Rav's time, since Rav appointed him over Babylonia's pursi. How could Meri also have lived so long? Therefore R.Ḥ.'s [ר״ח; provisionally Rabbenu Ḥananel] reading in Yevamot—also in the Arukh—seems right: Rav Ashi declared Rav Meri bar Raḥel fit. (Yevamot 92b has Rav Meri bar Raḥel say to Rav Ashi, 'Thus Amemar said.') Although Rav Ashi was born on the day Rava died, Meri could have been young in Rava's time, then great in Torah and old in Rav Ashi's, when he appointed him over Babylonia's pursi. End of Tosafot.

But Tosafot's assertion that Meri bar Raḥel was young in Rava's days is difficult for me. Wherever Meri bar Raḥel is mentioned with Rava, he appears grown in Rava's days; examine the passages above. I shall further show that he was born at least approximately thirteen or fourteen years before Rava. Ta'anit 24b: Rav Meri, son of Shemuel's daughter, said, 'I saw angels filling boats with sand, which became flour.' Rashi says this was on the day Rav Yehudah prayed for rain (see his entry). Presumably Meri was grown when he saw this, since a minor's testimony is not accepted; even a ten-year-old is called a minor (see there; see R. Elazar son of R. Tzadok). Rava was born when Rav Yehudah died, and was Abaye's contemporary in age (see his entry). He became head after Abaye's death and led for fourteen years afterward. Abaye lived sixty years, so Rava lived approximately seventy-four. Rav Ashi was born when Rava died and was presumably grown when he declared Meri fit for appointment. Even if Meri was thirteen or fourteen when Rav Yehudah died and the angels' incident occurred near that death, Meri would have been over a hundred when Rav Ashi appointed him: fourteen at Rav Yehudah's death, seventy-four of Rava's life, and at least eighteen of Rav Ashi's at the appointment. How could he live so long?

This was Tosafot's objection, yet its own difficulty was smaller. Rav died in 4003, Rav Yehudah in 4058 or 4060 (see part 1): fifty-five or fifty-seven years apart. Rav could have appointed Meri over Babylonia's pursi at life's end, when Meri was twenty. At all Meri's dealings with Rava, Rava too could have been twenty. Meri's twenty at appointment, plus Rav Yehudah's fifty-five or fifty-seven remaining years, plus Rava's twenty, total ninety-five or ninety-seven. Why erase 'Rav declared him fit' for that reason? They should instead erase it because even if Rav appointed him at life's end, Meri would then be no younger than twenty; add fifty-five or fifty-seven until Rav Yehudah's death, seventy-four of Rava's life, and Rav Ashi's birth and at least fifteen years before Meri told him 'Thus Amemar said': Meri before Rav Ashi would have been at least 164! They have left me room, thank God, to distinguish myself. Under Tosafot's reading 'Rav Ashi declared him fit,' Meri was over a hundred: fourteen at the angels' incident during Rav Yehudah's fast, even at Rav Yehudah's life's end, when Rava was born; Rava's seventy-four years; and at least fifteen of Rav Ashi's at appointment—over a hundred.

In my opinion Rav Ashi is also an incorrect reading. Meri was certainly extremely old in Rav Ashi's days for appointment over Babylonia's pursi. The Arukh, under Parhedrin, interprets this as agardemin, a superintendent of markets. In fact, Sefer M.E. [מ״ע; provisionally Me'or Einayim] disagrees, interpreting it as counselors and a court like the Sanhedrin. That is plainly difficult, since an old man is not appointed to the Sanhedrin (see R. Eliezer the Great). The reading 'Rava declared him fit' therefore seems more correct. 'Rav declared him fit' would then lack only a mark: it was written רב׳, meaning Rava; the mark was erased, leaving Rav. A Rav Ashi reading, however, would require an entire word to have dropped out in printing—רב אשי [the source's formulation retained]. R״Sh [unresolved writer] writes at Bava Metzia 73: perhaps after Issur's death Raḥel married Rabbah, making Rabbah Meri bar Raḥel's stepfather, like ben Kenaz, Kenaz's stepson. Rav Meri, son of Shemuel's daughter, said, 'Thus Abaye said,' Bava Metzia 110a. Rav Aḥa Sava, Mar Zutra and Rabbah were Rav Meri's sons (see their entries).
